blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The point-biserial coefficient r_pb is Pearson’s r between a continuous variable and a binary variable coded 0/1. The phi coefficient φ is Pearson’s r between two binary variables coded 0/1; from a 2 × 2 table, φ = √(χ² ÷ N) in size.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Neither needs a new formula: code the binary variable 0/1 and compute r. The names survive from the days of hand calculation.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
In the CBHI survey (500 households, 150 members), members live on average 6.41 km from the facility and non-members 8.12 km; the SD of distance is 3.25 km. Coding membership 1/0:

r_pb = [(ȳ₁ − ȳ₀) ÷ s_y] × √[p(1 − p)] × √[n/(n − 1)] = (−1.71 ÷ 3.25) × √(0.30 × 0.70) × 1.001 = −0.24

Its t = r√(n − 2)/√(1 − r²) = 5.54 on 498 df is identical in size to the pooled two-sample t-test comparing mean distance between members and non-members (recall §9.2.2): the two analyses are one.

For phi, take the breastfeeding cohort of §10.6.4 (200 infants; χ² = 23.37): φ = √(23.37 ÷ 200) = 0.34.

points.html: The point-biserial t-test and the two-sample t-test give the same p-value; report whichever the reader will understand (usually the difference in means).

φ can reach ±1 only when the two variables have the same marginal proportions, so it is a poor guide to strength. For a 2 × 2 table the risk ratio or odds ratio (recall §10.6.4) is usually the more useful summary.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 11.1

questions.prompt: For 10 women, Sₓₓ = 250, S_yy = 40 and Sₓᵧ = 80 (haemoglobin in g/dL against daily iron tablets taken over a month). Compute the covariance, r and the t statistic for H₀: ρ = 0. Is r significant at the 5% level?
questions.answer:
1. Covariance = Sₓᵧ ÷ (n − 1) = 80 ÷ 9 = 8.89.
  2. r = Sₓᵧ ÷ √(Sₓₓ × S_yy) = 80 ÷ √(250 × 40) = 80 ÷ √10,000 = 80 ÷ 100 = 0.80.
  3. t = r√(n − 2) ÷ √(1 − r²) = 0.80 × √8 ÷ √0.36 = 2.263 ÷ 0.60 = 3.77 on 8 df.
  4. The two-sided 5% critical value of t on 8 df is 2.306. 3.77 > 2.306, so r is significant (p = 0.005). With only 10 women, the association says nothing yet about cause: women who take more tablets may differ in diet or adherence to other advice.

questions.prompt: A study of 28 anganwadi workers reports r = 0.50 between years of service and a knowledge score. Compute the 95% confidence interval for ρ by Fisher’s z.
questions.answer:
1. z = ½ ln[(1 + 0.50) ÷ (1 − 0.50)] = ½ ln 3 = 0.549.
  2. SE(z) = 1 ÷ √(n − 3) = 1 ÷ √25 = 0.200.
  3. Limits on the z scale: 0.549 ± 1.96 × 0.200 = 0.157 to 0.941.
  4. Back-transform with r = (e²ᶻ − 1) ÷ (e²ᶻ + 1): 0.16 to 0.74.

The interval is wide and asymmetric about 0.50: the data fit anything from a weak to a strong association.

questions.prompt: A researcher correlates ranked examination scores with hours of study. Which coefficient(s) should she use, and why?
questions.answer: A rank coefficient: Spearman’s ρₛ or Kendall’s τ. Examination rank is ordinal (the gaps between ranks are not equal), so Pearson’s r, which uses the actual distances from the mean, is not appropriate. Both rank coefficients use only order. Spearman’s ρₛ is Pearson’s r on the ranks; Kendall’s τ is the proportion of concordant minus discordant pairs. Either is acceptable; report which one, since their values are on different scales.
